title: How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections
text:
A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​

Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country.

"This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast", the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.

The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.

Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it.

"I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC.

A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernaut

A new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators.

Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.

There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by , external Pew Research Center.

Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.

Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand.

"This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."

Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US Senator working on data centre legislation.

"There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."

That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.

Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".

His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.

The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.

During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.

Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the push back against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago.

"People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."

New national polling , external shows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran War and various aspects of the economy.

Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.

Yet, recent research , external from Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.

Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centres project.

Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.

Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.

In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees.

Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position. Recent polls , external have found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should be up to local citizens and elected officials.

Meanwhile, Brown has stumped on his opposition to new data centres. He leads Husted in recent polls.…

title: As Christmas rush looms, how do China-made toys find their way to the US?
text:
On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".

Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external

Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external

With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.

As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.

Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.

In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.

The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.

Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America

Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.

Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."

Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.

So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.

On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.

Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.

Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.

He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."

And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.

Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report , external at the start of this year.

Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.

The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.

Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.

From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.

Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.

Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.

Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.

Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.

This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.

This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.

"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.

The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.

That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.

"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.

If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.

While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.…

title: How much is the minimum wage?
text:
The official minimum rates of pay rose for 2.7 million workers on 1 April.

The rate for workers aged 21 and over is called the National Living Wage, while those aged 18 to 20 are paid the National Minimum Wage.

From 1 April 2026, workers over 21 on the National Living Wage are paid £12.71 an hour, 50p more than in 2025.

For someone working full time (37.5 hours a week), that amounts to £24,784.50 a year - an increase of £900.

The rate for 18 to 20-year-olds has gone up to £10.85 an hour.

It amounts to an increase of £1,500 a year for a full-time worker.

The government said its goal is to eventually scrap this separate rate for 18 to 20-year-olds, and have one rate for all adults.

The minimum wage for 16 and 17-year-olds has also risen to £8 an hour.

There are different rates of pay for apprentices , external depending on their age and what stage of apprenticeship they are in.

Apprentices aged 16 to 18 are entitled to the National Minimum Wage rate for that age group which is currently £8.

Those aged 19, or in the first year of their apprenticeship, are paid the same amount.

But those over 19 - or who have already completed their first year - are entitled to the appropriate National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage rate for their age.

What is an apprenticeship and how much is the pay?

Some workers do not qualify for either the National Minimum Wage or the National Living Wage.

This includes the self-employed, company directors, volunteers, members of the armed forces and prisoners.

People with disabilities or in long-term unemployment who take part in government work programmes are paid fixed amounts at different stages of the scheme.

These are less than the equivalent National Minimum or Living rate.

Yes. It is a criminal offence for employers not to pay the correct National Minimum and Living Wages to eligible employees.

The rates apply even if workers are not paid by the hour.

Calculator: Am I getting the right wage? , external

If you think you are being paid the wrong amount, you can complain via the HMRC website , external .

You can also get advice from workplace experts Acas , external .

Any employer not paying the correct amount can be penalised by HMRC.

In March 2026, the government said that 389 employers had been fined around £12.6m for failing to pay staff properly , external .

They must also repay the missing £7.3m to the around 60,000 workers who were underpaid.

Firm named included the Nursery chain Busy Bees , Norwich City Football Club, Hays Travel and Costa Coffee.

The Real Living Wage , external is an unofficial hourly rate of pay which is overseen by the Living Wage Foundation charity, who say it is set at a rate to meet the cost of living.

Some firms choose to pay the Real Living Wage, but it is not mandatory.

According to the charity almost 500,000 employees working for nearly 17,000 firms receive the voluntary rate of pay.

In October 2026, the foundation said the UK rate would increase by 4.8% to £14.10 an hour, while the London Living Wage for workers in the capital would go up by 4.4% to £15.45.

The Living Wage Foundation says the rate is worth over £2,700 more per year than the legal minimum wage in the UK, and over £5,300 more in London.

title: Outburst came out of 'anger and frustration' - Martinez
text:
Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez says he "spoke out of anger and frustration" when launching a scathing attack on the club's hierarchy.

The Argentina international criticised United for not strengthening the squad in the summer following qualification for the Champions League in comments made after the 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid in the Champions League group phase on Tuesday.

Martinez said he expected more investment in the United squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]".

However, while he stopped short of an apology, he said he has "belief in my team-mates, our manager [Michael Carrick] and everyone working to help this club move forward".

"After the match, I spoke out of anger and frustration at not getting the result we all wanted," he wrote in a social media post.

"Those who know me know how I live football, with passion, commitment and a huge desire to win. And when things don't go our way, it hurts, especially when representing a club with the history and stature of Manchester United .

"My words reflect how I feel and how much I want to see this club competing for the biggest honours.

"Those high standards are part of how I see football and the responsibility that comes with wearing this shirt.

"When I talk about wanting more, I'm talking about the ambition we must all have as part of this club.

"To keep growing, to become stronger and to have everything we need to compete at the highest level.

"These are standards we must all hold ourselves to, starting with me."

Man Utd defender Martinez issues scathing attack on board

Wilcox the target again in another damaging Man Utd fallout

Manchester United have not won in five games since beating Sabah in the Champions League on 10 September.

They have won just two of their nine games this season and are 13th in the Premier League with six points from as many games.

Martinez's contract expires at the end of the season and United have the option to extend it by another year.

He added: "I know that, first and foremost, it's us, the players, who have to deliver, and I put myself at the front of that responsibility.

"We need to demand even more of ourselves and work together to take Manchester United back to the top.

"I believe in my teammates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward.

"I'm convinced that the way forward is to keep working together, with ambition and commitment.

"My goal has been the same since day one, to win, compete at the highest level and to give everything I have for this badge."

Manchester United 's next game will be at Leeds United in the Premier League on Sunday, 18 October.

title: Manchester United teammates widely share Martínez view that Wilcox is failing
author: Jamie Jackson
text:
Defender voiced criticism after defeat at Atlético

Martínez out of contract next summer and plans to leave

Lisandro Martínez’s view that Jason Wilcox is failing as Manchester United’s director of football reflects the dressing room’s general frustration at recruitment and squad depth, although the outburst is also regarded as a push by the defender to secure a move because he is out of contract next summer.

Martínez’s comments came after Tuesday’s 2-0 Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid . This left United with two wins all season, having taken six points from their first six Premier League matches, the club’s poorest league start for 40 years.

The run of form has placed Michael Carrick’s position under pressure, but Martínez zoned in on Wilcox and the rest of the hierarchy. “Tonight it is easy to say the coach, easy to say the players, but also we have to see other areas,” he said, pointing upwards.

“I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]. I have to be honest, as players we have to do more, but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.”

Wilcox, the executive in charge of transfers, oversaw a £155m spend in the last window on Youri Tielemans , Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba . The decision to recruit three midfielders and not strengthen other areas has been met with puzzlement within the squad, particularly as Wilcox sought a left-back, with Newcastle’s Lewis Hall the prime target.

Luke Shaw is United’s only senior player in that position and his 12-year career at the club has been plagued by injury. The 31-year-old missed the Atlético defeat and Saturday’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham owing to a muscular problem. The lack of depth at left-back reflects the prevailing view among players that Carrick has been left without the resources to challenge. United were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brighton after making eight changes.

Although Carrick led United to third last season, this came after he took over as caretaker in mid-January with only 17 league games to play with the team out of all the other competitions.

Martínez is understood to favour a move, ideally to an elite European club outside the Premier League.

title: Monumental year takes US rising star Ashlin Barry from 'I could barely walk' to 'memory that will last a lifetime'
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
New under-23 road world champion Ashlin Barry didn't have a lot of time to celebrate a gold medal and a rainbow jersey as one of the most extraordinary rewards for a 19th birthday three weeks ago. After his solo conquest across the slopes of Mont Royal in the U23 road race at the UCI Road World Championships, he went straight to Los Angeles for a training camp on the track with Team USA and then headed to Shanghai for the UCI Track World Championships .

There's no time to rest on any laurels for Barry, as his sights are set on a version of California dreaming at the Los Angeles Olympic Games, now 639 days away.

"At the moment, I'm putting a lot of focus on the track in Team Pursuit, and then maybe qualifying for the Omnium, or something will come as a byproduct of that. If I could qualify for the road [at the Olympic Games], that would be pretty cool. But I think I have to take a step up physically from where I am now to make that selection," Barry told in an exclusive one-on-one interview in Montréal.

"In terms of preparation, there's a lot going into our team pursuit now, and whether it's like a bunch event on the track or qualifying for the road, I think those will fall into place."

Barry has a huge balancing act to manage across multiple disciplines, global travel and a new commitment through 2029 to the Visma-Lease a Bike Development squad that could see him jump to the WorldTour team sooner rather than later.

Just two years before, he impressed with a silver medal in the Omnium at the Junior Track World Championships, sweeping US national titles in the road race and time trial, and winning junior and elite national titles in the Madison.

In 2025, after graduating from high school, he came second in the junior men's E3 Saxo Classic and Paris-Roubaix, earned a silver medal in the junior time trial at World Roads and the gold medal in the US Pro junior time trial national championships.

But his plan to make a statement on the track was derailed at the start of 2026, and he kept goals with his new Visma team modest.

"This was a tough year because I was supposed to do Pan Am Championships in February. I crashed on my knee in January, so I wasn't able to ride my bike. I could barely walk," he recalled.

"Things didn't go as planned. I was in Spain at training camp. Then I had to get some stitches in my knee, and I couldn't bend it. It could have been a lot worse, but it was a couple of weeks off the bike, and then I missed the track because of that."

While his track maturation was put on hold in the spring, he jumped into the fray in the Olympia's Tour at the end of March, earning two podiums. He then finished fifth in the U23 In Flanders Fields and then won the US Pro U23 road race and came in fourth in the US Pro elite men's road race the next day.

So when he finished one step off the podium in the U23 time trial at Montreal Road Worlds, he had modest expectations yet again. When asked two days before the U23 road race what he expected, the teen simply stated that he could be competitive on Friday but was "not going in thinking I have a super-high chance of getting a medal".

A gold medal and rainbow jersey were the result of a solo ride on his biggest stage yet. Barry called the win in the men's U23 road race "a memory that will last a lifetime". It was a monumental final 30 kilometres of the 174km contest, as the teenager carried the colours of Team USA to the win, and enthralled family and friends from two countries as a dual citizen of the US and Canada.

Even as he held his pace at the front of the race for the 12th of 13 circuits across Mont Royal, he said he wasn't sure he was strong enough to maintain a 40-second advantage. However, once he crested the major climb the final time and added to his solo lead, he let himself believe he could win, encouraged by supporters around the course.

"Once I was away, I just committed. It really felt like a home race out there," he told the media, including , in Montreal. "It was just unreal being out there, seeing so many friends, seeing my family. I could hear my dog barking on the side of the course."

He now registers an entry in the family's journal of success in Montreal, his mother and former US elite women's road race national champion Dede Demet-Barry having won a pro race in Montreal in 2002, five years before Barry was born. His father and two-time Canadian road race silver medallist Michael Barry competed on the Mont Royal course on two editions of Grand Prix du Cycliste Montreal, when his son was old enough to remember ringing a cowbell at his father's race.

Both parents competed at multiple road world championships for their respective countries; Michael's best effort was eighth in the U23 road race in 1996, while Dede won the junior road title in 1989. And Dede also competed frequently on the track, going fourth at the UCI Junior World Track Championships.

Demet-Barry later translated that speed to a silver medal on the road at the Athens Olympic Games in the individual time trial. An Olympic medal of any colour, and in road or track, has the attention of her son.

Barry said one of the reasons he enjoys the track so much is the emphasis on teamwork, be it Team Pursuit and other events like Madison. In fact, his personal favourite moment from 2025 was not even a win, but a fourth-place finish.

"[Last year] at Track Worlds, we were just off the cusp of getting a medal. But seeing the way that programme's come together has been really cool, and I'm personally proud to be a part of it, proud of those guys and seeing the way they've improved," he said about the US Men's Team Pursuit squad.

"[Track] Worlds will be a really good opportunity for me, and then I'm hoping next year to do Track Worlds again, hoping to get some more racing experience on the track."

This year, the quest for a gold medal in Team Pursuit began on the first day of the 2026 UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai as Barry rejoined Grant Koontz and Anders Johnson with the new addition of Taylor Phinney. They made it through qualifying but not the first round, with France ending their dreams. Barry will race the individual pursuit and Elimination Race later this week.

On the road, before earning his world title, Barry said his top road highlight of the season also showed the teamwork he values.

"There's something special about achieving something with another person or with a group of people, and being able to share that moment. The Olympia story comes to mind. That was just a cool moment, I mean one-two is cool," Barry said about that March race with teammates on the podium.

"We had a great team there. It's a good atmosphere; I really liked that course. I feel proud about the way that I raced there and worked with my teammate Aldo.

"My teammate and I were in that front gro,up and probably we had a pretty equal chance of winning, either one of us. I mean, he was second in the end, but he helped me set up that winning attack. He could have gone to the finish and won. It just ended by luck that I was the one winning."

Barry has the talent, not just the luck. Those two top moments of the past two seasons, however, were probably pushed to runner-up positions after he won the U23 road world championship.

In fact, his personal victory was also one for his country, scoring the country's first-ever U23 world title for a US athlete. And who was the last U23 men's rider to take a medal of any colour? It was his track teammate Taylor Phinney in 2010, who tied Canadian Guillaume Boivin to give the USA a bronze.

title: 'Same start time, same distance, same energy' - Charlotte Kool calls out Eneco Tour on unequal prize list
author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
text:
However, their focus on equity hasn't made its way to the prize purse, a point that sprint leader Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) pointed out on Instagram. She posted an image of the prize list, which shows the women are racing for a total of €17,205 while the men's purse is €63,465.

"I'm curious if women get a discount at @eneco for energy? Prologue: Same start time, same distance, same energy," Kool wrote in the post.

While men's prologue winner Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) pocketed €1,490 for his effort, women's winner Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) earned just €220. Tim Merlier (Soudal-Quickstep) will take home €3,060 for winning the sprint on stage 1, while Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché) gained just €370.

Speaking to Kool expanded, saying, "It's not about the money for us; that is just a small bonus. It's more about the principle, that it's a bit strange.

"It was a bit of a joke," she said of her post. "Because it is of course a bit skewed that, as the Eneco Tour, you promote that men and women are on equal footing, and then there is such a difference in prize money."

During the 2020 season, Flanders Classics, organisers of the Tour of Flanders and other races, launched an initiative called ' Closing the Gap ' to bring more parity to broadcast coverage and prize money. The Tour of Flanders awarded equal prizes in 2022, and Flanders Classics extended that to five other races in 2023.

But events like the Tour de France still give women a tenth of what the men earn, so the fight is not over yet.

title: No Medal Ride for Taylor Phinney as USA Team Pursuit Starts Road to LA 2028
author: ahood
text:
Phinney, right, competed in track worlds in China. (Photo: Sean M. Haffey/Getty Image)

Taylor Phinney ’s return to the track ended short of the medal rounds Wednesday as Team USA finished seventh in the men’s team pursuit in the Shanghai UCI Track Cycling World Championships .

But all is not lost as the team opens a long, 18-month fight to earn one of eight qualifying spots for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games .

Phinney, newly crowned U23 road world champion Ashlin Barry , Grant Koontz and Anders Johnson clocked 3:50.916 in the second leg of racing.

The Americans led early against France but lost their heat by 1.297 seconds, posting the seventh-fastest time among the eight teams.

France advanced to Thursday’s bronze-medal final against Great Britain. Denmark and Italy will race for gold.

The Americans squeezed into the first round with a qualifying time of 3:51.029, finishing seventh among 18 nations and 6.038 seconds behind defending champion Denmark.

They shaved just over a tenth of a second off that mark in their second ride, while France found nearly two seconds to advance.

Also Wednesday, Team USA’s women’s team pursuit — racing without heavy hitters like Chloé Dygert and Jennifer Valente — stopped the clock in ninth, and missed qualifying for the medal rounds on Thursday.

Team USA and Phinney were hoping for more in one of the biggest American cycling’s biggest comeback stories this season .

For Phinney, a two-time individual pursuit world champion, Shanghai marked his first worlds since coming out of retirement to chase a spot at the home Olympics.

“This is my first race back. It feels good, it feels like coming home. It’s fun riding with the guys,” Phinney said before racing.

“We have a really strong team, but it’s a question mark coming into the race to understand where the other teams are at. If we can do a top 5, we’d be happy with that,” he said. “We will take it one round at a time”

The result fell short of that ambition and of the benchmark the American program set last year, when the squad was fourth in the 2025 worlds.

Team USA’s last worlds medals in team pursuit was bronze way back in 1995.

Phinney, 36, returns to a discipline that also looks radically different from when he raced in the 2008 Olympic Games in track.

“The technology has changed quite a lot, especially in team pursuit. If you look at my (body) position in the individual pursuit, it was completely wide open, and now everything is super closed,” he said. “I think the position is more extreme, but the power numbers, they’re not, like, so much different.”

Team USA’s men’s squad has a big mountain to climb to qualify for the Olympic Games.

While the women’s team pursuit won gold in Paris 2024 , the men didn’t even field a team and has never won an Olympic medal in team pursuit.

Phinney and rising star Barry give the squad new hope, but it won’t be easy.

Only eight nations per gender will qualify for the LA28 for team pursuit and the road to Los Angeles started Wednesday. The points window runs from this week at the Shanghai worlds through April 2028.

Seventh at these worlds provides an early marker to build on, but it’s far from guaranteeing a spot in Los Angeles.

Team USA will need to keep scoring against the same deep field across the qualifying World Cups, Pan American championships, and next year’s track worlds.

The next qualifying event to watch is the World Cup series, which starts April 2-4, 2027, in Milton, Canada. That’s followed by Hong Kong on April 23-25 and another Chinese round from April 30 to May 2.

The 2027 world championships provide another major test, with the track competition scheduled for August 26-30 at Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines as part of the “super worlds” set for France next summer.

For Phinney and the Americans, the first race is in the books.

Now comes the hard part of competing against the confirmed power houses like Denmark, Great Britain, Australia, and Italy, and finish inside the top eight to punch their ticket to Los Angeles.

title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story
author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
text:
Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers

The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”

Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.

Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.

She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”

Kundizeza responded in a statement on X : “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.

“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”

Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.

Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.

The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”

Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.

Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.

“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”

Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.

In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”

Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.

title: ‘I expect more’: the key questions from Martínez’s Manchester United broadside | Jamie Jackson
author: Jamie Jackson
text:
From Jason Wilcox’s role to the views of the rest of the squad, we tackle the major talking points at Old Trafford after the defender’s outburst

After Manchester United’s 2-0 loss at Atlético Madrid, Lisandro Martínez teed off at the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and the rest of the executive. “We don’t have the best squad at the moment compared with other top teams,” said the defender. “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox] … Really poor [the Atlético defeat] – I have to control myself a lot but something is a reflection of the mirror of how our club is at the moment.” Here we consider the key questions emerging from Martínez’s explosive remarks.

Yes is the short answer . The Guardian has been told the decision to target three midfielders in Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Carlos Baleba caused bemusement in the squad that no other areas were strengthened in the summer. Carrick led United to third last term after the side only had 17 league games remaining when he took over in January, having been eliminated from the other competitions. The need for defensive reinforcements is particularly acute because the back four of Diogo Dalot, Martínez, Harry Maguire and Luke Shaw has been together since 2022. Martínez is out of contract next summer and it is thought the 28-year-old may not be offered a new deal or have his one-year option triggered by the club, so teammates are conscious his outburst also came because he expects to leave.

As United’s director of football the 55-year-old wields near-unilateral power on football decisions, with only Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy, above him. If the buck stops with the executive, the most recent transfer window was Wilcox’s responsibility. This was the latest in a line of missteps on his United record. One concerns when Dan Ashworth (Wilcox’s predecessor) was on gardening leave from Newcastle in the first half of 2024 , Wilcox interviewed potential replacements for Erik ten Hag before, oddly, deeming that the head coach should stay . The Dutchman signed a fresh contract but was sacked that autumn . Another involves Wilcox’s major falling out with the man he hired as the Dutchman’s successor, Ruben Amorim, after which the Portuguese said the director of football had told him he should change his favoured 3-4-3 shape . “I came here to be the manager of Manchester United – not to be the coach of Manchester United,” said Amorim, after a 1-1 draw at Leeds on 4 January (his job title was head coach). He was sacked the next day. Wilcox worked with Omar Berrada, United’s chief executive, at Manchester City, where Berrada rose to become chief football operations officer, and Wilcox became academy director. Wilcox moved to Southampton and became director of football from summer 2023 until April 2024, when he joined United , having been identified by Berrada, so there is scrutiny of his experience at elite level.

The 45-year-old’s ability to prosper is related to the quality of Wilcox’s work, primarily in the market, so he cannot be solely responsible for a dire six points from six league games and two victories in all competitions all season. Yet by definition his role as head coach demands Carrick do the best with his resources, and that progress is made on the training ground. On matchdays there is scant excuse for United’s disjointedness, inferior running stats and inability, twice, to take advantage against 10 men: the 1-0 loss to City and Saturday’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham . How is Carrick viewed by his players? According to Santos they back him. “We believe in the manager, we believe in the whole staff, we believe in [ourselves as] players,” he said after the Atlético game. “We are in a bad moment but we have to work to change this result.”.

For further evidence see Amad Diallo’s Snapchat post after the defeat by Atlético: “Fucking disgrace; I have no words.” So United have a World Cup-winner, Martínez, aiming shots at Wilcox and by implication Ratcliffe and Berrada, and a fellow senior player, Diallo, cursing but in ambiguous fashion, adding to the sense of meltdown at the club because it is unclear whether the “disgrace” meant the performance, Martínez’s diatribe, the squad his teammate referred to as not good enough, or something else. All of this is mirrored on the pitch, where United’s 671.4km run in the Premier League is the fifth-lowest (Arsenal’s 716.2 is the highest), and their 581 sprints the fourth-lowest (Brentford’s 765 the most).

In mitigation Wilcox can point to the six American siblings, who remain majority owners and whose family has placed an eye-watering £1.1bn-plus debt on the club that severely restricts the transfer budget. Wilcox oversaw a £155m summer outlay and a net spend of about £100m in a summer when City’s corresponding figures were £457.5m and about £175m. City buying players such as Enzo Fernández (for a British record-equalling £125m), Elliot Anderson (£115m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (£81m) and Iliman Ndiaye (£65m) showed their greater financial muscle, helped by being much better sellers of talent. How they have reached this point has, though, been thrown into sharp focus by last month’s verdict that they have serially cheated.…

title: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
text:
Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years.

Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from £7 to £10.

Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from £6 to £8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from £5 to £8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City.

The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".

The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives".

The RAC, which conducted the analysis in July this year, has campaigned against increases in drop-off charges. It said a review of "kiss and fly" fees would be "music to the ears to drivers".

"We know airport drop-off charges are a growing source of anger and frustration," said Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC.

"Four-in-five drivers we've surveyed believe they are a 'rip-off', with just one-in-10 understanding why airports charge what they do."

The RAC's research found London City Airport, which only introduced charges in 2026, was the most expensive on a per-minute basis.

Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute. Belfast International Airport now charges £5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up £2 on last year.

None of the top 10 airports in the European Union charge for drop-offs, according to the RAC.

It argues that international airports should not charge for dropping off passengers, however, the industry said the charges were a neccesary part of the business model of airports.

Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest

Supporters of such charges also say they encourage travellers to use of more environmentally friendly modes of transport.

"Airports outside the UK are typically publicly owned and in receipt of state subsidies and tax exemptions, while UK airports are generally privately owned and subject to the full array of commercial rates of taxation," said Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, which represents airports.

She added airports offered a "range of options for those travelling to terminals, including free drop off points" and that "any review" by the government would find airports make "excellent use of a variety of ways to manage traffic and air pollution".

The Aviation Environment Federation campaign group has previously defended the fees, arguing they help reduce congestion and air pollution around airports.

Earlier this month, the government announced extra charges for parents sitting with their children when flying would be scrapped in time for next year's summer holidays.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the changes were part of a series of "everyday fixes" to ease cost of living pressures on households.

title: Netcompany Ineos sign 23-year-old former Tour de l'Avenir winner for 2027
author: Alasdair Fotheringham
text:
The young British racer joins Ineos after two years at NSN and Israel-Premier Tech, which followed a dramatically successful 2024 season that saw him win both the Tour de l’Avenir and the U23 Liège-Bastogne-Liège.

This year, however, Blackmore's racing has been severely disrupted by knee injuries, to the point where he took part in just three races and abandoned all of them. He did, however, complete the Tour de France in his first full season as a pro back in 2025, when he also claimed fourth in Brabantse Pijl in the same year.

Blackmore was one of three signings announced by Ineos Grenadiers on Wednesday, the other two being fellow Briton James Shaw and French climber Clément Champoussin.

“I’m extremely excited and grateful for the opportunity to spend the next three years of my career with Netcompany Ineos," Blackmore said in a team press release.

"It’s been a tough 2026 for me with injuries, but it’s made me even more motivated to reach my full potential.

“Joe is a rider we’ve followed closely, and someone we believe has significant potential," Netcompany Ineos director of racing Geraint Thomas added.

"He has already shown what he is capable of across different types of racing, but importantly we believe there is still a lot more to come."

Shaw, 30, has yet to take a win in his career, but with seven Grand Tours in his palmares, the Briton has built a solid reputation as a strong climber. Shaw is also well known for setting his career back on track after two initial pro seasons at Lotto were followed by three away from the WorldTour in smaller squads.

At a point where others would have thrown in the towel, Shaw made it back to the top level and has now raced for the last five years at EF Education-EasyPost. “As a kid, this [Ineos] was the team that inspired me," Shaw said.

"I grew up looking up to riders like Geraint Thomas, so to now have the opportunity to pull on the jersey and become part of a team I've admired for so long is a dream come true."

Also set to provide a boost to Netcompany Ineos climbing line-up in 2027, like Shaw, is 28-year-old Clément Champoussin , moving on from XDS-Astana to race with the British WorldTour team next season.

A former top-ten finisher in Paris-Nice and Itzulia Basque Country , Champoussin has signed a three-year deal through to 2029 with Netcompany Ineos. They will be his fourth professional team following spells as AG2R-Decathlon, Arkéa-Samsic and, most recently, two years at Astana.

This year a promising early start for Champoussin, including a fifth place overall at Itzulia Basque Country and top 20 placings in La Flèche Wallonne and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, was followed by a more uneven midseason. 2026 was the first time since 2022 that the Frenchman has not taken part in a single Grand Tour, where his best placing remains 16th overall in the Vuelta back in 2021.

“Clément brings significant experience and another dimension to the group," Thomas added about the Frenchman, originally from Nice, but now reportedly a resident in Andorra.

"He's a solid, strong and consistent climber who has shown he can perform at the highest level.

In a busy transfer season for Netcompany Ineos, the British squad is set to see multiple significant departures and arrivals this winter. Amongst those departing are Italian time trial giant Filippo Ganna, Americans AJ August and Magnus Sheffield, British allrounder Ben Swift, who is retiring, and Australian sprinter Sam Welsford.

Meanwhile, Champoussin, Shaw and Blackmore are three of the seven riders currently confirmed to be heading the opposite direction, with others joining Ineos including Champoussin's current XDS-Astana teammate, Harold Tejada, and the teenage Spanish star and double junior World Champion, Benjamin Noval.

title: 'I was deliberately pushed into the barriers' – Guarischi relegated from Eneco Tour sprint after complaints from Kool
author: James Moultrie
text:
Barbara Guarischi (SD Worx-Protime) has been relegated for her sprint on stage 1 of the Eneco Tour , after her actions left Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech), the rider she hampered in the final 150 metres, furious at the finish line on Wednesday.

Kool was the favourite for the flat stage in Ede, and was well placed on the wheel of the Italian rider coming out of the final corner. As Guarischi launched her sprint in the middle of the road, Kool began to launch on her left, only for the Italian rider to close her to the barrier, causing the Dutch rider to take evasive action and restart her sprint on the other side.

By the time she was back up to speed, Kool had already lost the stage to Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché), turning back and throwing her hand in the air at Guarischi for her actions in the sprint. Kool didn't mince her words when she spoke after the stage.

"I'm just really bummed that as a team we're sacrificing everything to let it come down to a sprint; you just want a fair chance," said Kool to Dutch publication .

"I think that fair chance has been taken away from me now. I find that very unsportsmanlike and very unfortunate.

"I haven't seen it back yet, but in my view, I was deliberately and intentionally pushed into the barriers. It wasn't just a little bit of a deviation from the line; it went from right to left. So yes, I find that very unsportsmanlike.

"Everyone knows images from the past. That goes through your head. I really want to win, but not much. And I also know that she won't give up easily, because she didn't do that to begin with."

The official results initially showed no consequences for Guarischi's sprint, but a post on AG Insurance Soudal's social media pages later on Wednesday evening confirmed that the Italian had been relegated, putting her at the back of the bunch in 85th.

"Nicola Steigenga has been promoted to third place in the final race classification of the first stage, following a race incident and the subsequent disqualification of the rider initially classified in third place," read a post from AG Insurance Soudal.

While the results page on the Eneco Tour's website has, at the time of writing, not been updated with the relegation for Guarischi, it is likely she was deemed to have broken rule 2.3.036 of the UCI regulations: "Riders shall be strictly forbidden to deviate from the lane they selected when launching into the sprint and, in so doing, obstructing or endangering others."

title: Red Bull F1 boss Mekies gets new deal to 2031
text:
Red Bull have extended the contract of team principal Laurent Mekies until the end of 2031.

The Frenchman has led the team since he replaced Christian Horner following the Briton's sacking in the summer of 2025 after 20 years in charge.

After a difficult start to the 2026 season, Red Bull have improved their car to the extent that Max Verstappen has taken dominant victories in the last two races, in Malaysia and Singapore.

A statement attributed to the two main shareholders of Red Bull, Thai Chalerm Yoovidhya and Austrian Mark Mateschitz, said: "Laurent has played a crucial role in guiding the team through an important period of transition while maintaining the competitive spirit and the Red Bull principles that define us.

"This extension reflects our confidence in his leadership and our shared belief in the long-term vision of the team.

"We are ambitious about what lies ahead and we are committed to building on this momentum together."

The move comes less than two months after Verstappen extended his own contract with Red Bull by two years to the end of 2030 after a period of uncertainty over his future.

Verstappen's two victories came in the wake of an interview Horner gave to the Times in which he claimed Red Bull had "lost its mojo, its presence, its vibe".

Oliver Mintzlaff, who is in charge of the Red Bull F1 programme in his role as chief executive officer of corporate projects and investments, said: "Laurent has demonstrated outstanding leadership since returning to the Red Bull family. He combines technical expertise, strategic thinking, and a deep understanding of what makes our team successful.

"Just as importantly, he embodies the values and mentality that define the Red Bull way: courage, teamwork, determination, and an unrelenting desire to compete at the highest level.

"Continuity in leadership is a key ingredient for sustained success."

Mekies said: "I am incredibly proud to continue this journey with Red Bull Racing, and I would like to thank Chalerm, Mark, and Oliver, the entire team, and everyone involved for the trust they have placed in the project.

"What makes this team special is the way everyone comes together in pursuit of the same goal, and I feel privileged to work alongside such a talent and committed group every day."

title: Taylor Phinney's return from retirement in UCI Track World Championships fizzles as US men miss finals in team pursuit
author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
text:
The highly-anticipated return of 2010 pursuit world champion Taylor Phinney to international competition at the UCI Track World Championships as the starter for Team USA's men's team pursuit squad ended on day 1, the quartet missing the medal finals. It's a step backward for the team, who finished fourth in last year's championships in Santiago, Chile.

Phinney made a late decision to join the USA Cycling programme , announcing his return in April, more than six years after he quit professional cycling at age 29 in 2019. His aim was to make the team for the Los Angeles Olympic Games to emulate his parents Davis Phinney and Connie Carpenter-Phinney, who both earned medals at the last Olympics there in 1984.

"The track was where I first found love and success in this sport, it was even the first discipline to break my heart when my specialty event, the individual pursuit, was removed from the Olympic programme, which prompted me to swiftly abandon the track and go all in on the road," Phinney wrote in April.

"Recently, the USA boys have been making huge strides in the Team Pursuit, and I couldn't be more stoked to be joining them in the chase for the Olympic Dream."

Phinney joined Ashlin Barry, Grant Koontz and Anders Johnson for the Team Pursuit on Wednesday, stepping in for last year's team member Graeme Frislie, who will compete in the Omnium, Madison and Scratch Race.

Speaking to the UCI on Wednesday before racing started in the Shanghai Velodrome on Chongming Island, Phinney said being back at the highest level on the track "feels like coming home in a lot of ways".

"It's really fun to ride with the guys," he said. "The technology has changed quite a lot, especially in team pursuiting.

"The positions have changed a lot. If you look at my position in the individual pursuit from 2009 - it was like completely wide open, and now everything is super close. So I think the position is more extreme, but the power numbers, they are not like so much different.

"I'm also racing as the starter, so I take a lot of the first minute of the race, getting everybody up to speed. I mean, we have a really strong team. It's kind of a question mark coming into the race, trying to understand where the other teams are at."

Phinney was realistic about the team's chances, saying before the race: "If we could do a top five, I think we would be really happy with that. And if we go into the finals, then we are more than stoked. But we'll take it one every one round at a time."

While the team did enough in the qualifying round to move on to the next heat, which determined the teams for the medal finals, they were unable to advance, setting times two seconds slower than the team did in 2025 and missing the medal round by half a second.

title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
text:
Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.

The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.

Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".

The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.

In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".

Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount .

Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources."

Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon".

The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October.

Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.

The firm has been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films.

However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer.

He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau.

"Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said.

The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

title: Red Bull's F1 boss gets well-timed endorsement with extended deal
