title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
text:
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".

As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.

The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).

Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.

Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".

The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.

Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.

Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.

But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.

On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.

A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.

The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.

When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.

In a post on X , external , OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".

It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."

Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.

Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.

"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."

Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."

On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.

If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

title: Why Anyone Would Pay $6,500 for Great Wheels When $1,399 Gets You Really Close
author: Josh Ross
text:
Welcome to Dropped , a new weekly road and gravel cycling newsletter from Velo that brings you the latest ideas we’re debating endlessly on group rides, and a look behind the scenes of our coverage.

When Tom Pidcock showed up at the UCI Road World Championships riding a set of wheels with a bright white logo that few people had seen and even fewer had ridden, everyone started talking. Those in the industry knew the logo, though. I’d had long conversations with the brand, Partington, a year earlier about those exact wheels, and I knew right away that they were both exceptionally expensive and very rare.

Mostly though, those $6,500 Partington R-Series Performance Ti wheels got me thinking. In a moment when you can get great wheels for about 1/5th that price with specs that almost match, the Partingtons are a beacon. They don’t just represent genius engineering—although they are impressive on that front. They represent next-level marketing. Those wheels showing up under Pidcock at Worlds are a blueprint for how Western brands are still able to compete even when the pricing floor disappears.

The Partington R-Series Performance Ti in the 65mm depth is likely the wheelset Pidcock was on. There’s a possibility it’s the 50mm version (we weren’t able to get up close and personal with Pidcock’s bike to confirm), but for the sake of this article I’m focusing on the 65. I find it a more interesting wheel anyway. It’s 65mm deep with a sealed rim bed, a 23mm internal width, a 34mm external width, and a weight of 1,265 grams.

Just to be clear: those are absurdly impressive specs. Only a handful of wheels exist with anything close, and I’m not sure any quite match it across the board. The already high-end Zipp 454 NSW would have been the natural alternative—since he races on Zipp wheels for his Pinarello-Q 36.5 trade team—but it is shallower and about 100 grams heavier.

As for how they ride, I may get the chance to tell you firsthand in the future. For now, it’s irrelevant to the point I’m making. Assume the wheelset rides well—I’m certain it does, and it damn well better for $6,500.

You know what else likely rides well, though? The Elitewheels Drive SL 58D CS for $1,399. That wheelset has a 25mm internal width, a 36mm front / 34mm rear external width, a 58mm depth, and weighs 1,330 grams. Granted, you’ll probably have to tape the rim bed yourself. But at that price, you can wipe off the excess sealant with a hundred-dollar bill and still be well ahead.

And Elitewheels is just one of many Chinese brands making competitive wheelsets, frames, and components at a fraction of the cost of Western brands.

This is where I see things getting really interesting. When you look at the Elitewheels website, the marketing is, compared to Western brands, a bit bare bones. The Drive SL wheelset is shown as a 3D render on a generic black background. There are a couple of views, but they are essentially the same aside from a measurement drawing. There’s no aspirational images of riders using the wheels in the Swiss Alps, or wheels in a high-tech testing facility.

At Partington, you are greeted with an entirely different approach. You’ve probably already seen the wheels being used by Pidcock on the biggest stage in road racing, signifying the brand’s performance credentials. Then when you visit the website, you first see an image of a rider in a beautiful setting, actual images of the wheels, and an in-depth explanation and backstory about what sets the wheels apart.

Both wheelsets use carbon spokes, but whereas Elitewheels has nothing more to say about its spokes, the Partington wheels use “FLEXON” carbon spokes with a description about the kind of carbon they’re made of. Then there is the hub. Both are titanium, but the Elitewheels hub is simply a “one-piece titanium freehub” that “delivers instant engagement.” The Partington hub? That is a “PERFORM hub” engineered “using detailed Finite Element Analysis (FEA) to refine structural geometry, reduce mass while maintaining stiffness and ensuring efficient load transfer in real world conditions.” That sounds very special, right? Except every major manufacturer uses FEA.

Or maybe you really want to know about the details of the packaging. Don’t worry, Partington has you covered: “Wheels are packed individually in lithographically printed telescope-style boxes featuring a matte cellophane finish with spot UV varnish. Each wheel is held securely in a vacuum‑molded insert.” As someone who spent a decade as a print designer, I know exactly what that means. To most people, it is a completely irrelevant detail described in the most technical way possible. You either pretend you know what it is or simply believe it must be incredibly special. Elitewheels does not tell you about the packaging, in case you were wondering.

None of this is a bad thing, and the point here isn’t to drag Partington. The R-Series wheels genuinely represent incredible engineering with tangible differences from the competition.

Instead, the point is that Partington is walking the fine line of luxury performance. The brand is selling you on the idea of incredible performance in the exact same way Lamborghini does. It’s likely not performance you need (a Toyota can hit the speed limit all the same), and it might not even be performance everyday riders like you and me can realistically feel compared to the competition (again, I’ll see when I finally ride them), but the conversation has to start with performance.

That performance is only the foundation, though. Once it’s established, it’s time for the heritage and craftsman story to take over. You aren’t just buying a wheel from a factory brand like Zipp (never mind that those wheels are hand-built, too); you are buying an artisan product from a visionary founder manufacturing in Australia. Sure, it’s a highly technical bike wheel, but it’s also functional art, and that is the key.…

title: Jason Wilcox: ‘best eyes’ at Manchester United or promoted too far and too fast?
author: Will Unwin
text:
Director of football is tarnished by recruitment record and Amorim stint but has received glowing review from above

L isandro Martínez is not naive. At 28, he has experienced plenty in football and knows the causes of success and failure. He has a World Cup winner’s medal , whereas Jason Wilcox has overseen the latest period of mediocrity at Manchester United, during which the focus has fallen more on the team’s performances than the wider reasons behind it.

Martínez was not solely speaking for himself when, after United’s defeat at Atlético Madrid, he strongly criticised Wilcox. His views are shared by others at United frustrated by the output from above and who “expect” more from a director of football. Wilcox knows he is under pressure because the inadequate results cannot all be pinned on Michael Carrick, who is working with a squad unable to cope with the rigours of challenging at the top of the Premier League and facing Europe’s elite.

Clubs live and die by their recruitment, and United sitting 13th in the Premier League after one win from six matches does not suggest the squad is in rude health. A sporting director, like a referee, goes unnoticed when performing well but it has reached the point at United where players can take no more.

Three years at Ajax taught Martínez about football structure. The Dutch clubs mix homegrown players with imports from around the world, many of whom are sold on for large profits. Wilcox would struggle to make the case that any of his recruits, with the possible exception of Senne Lammens, have markedly increased in value. There are many sporting directors more adept at finding undervalued talent. Wilcox was offered the chance to sign Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest a year before the midfielder signed for Manchester City , but decided against moving for a player who continued to grow in value and was eventually out of United’s price range. If Sir Jim Ratcliffe is so eager to run United as a business, questioning why the outlay on players leads to so little return would be a sensible starting point.

Wilcox arrived at Old Trafford in April 2024 after less than a year as the director of football in the Championship with Southampton, who gave him his first executive role in senior football. Before that, the former Blackburn and Leeds winger had worked in youth development, eventually becoming Manchester City’s academy director, and was well respected, but whether this was sufficient grounding for leading United’s football operation was debatable. Wilcox oversaw at City the emergence of a glut of talent, including Phil Foden, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers. Some of those who have dealt with him feel a senior academy position is where his skills lie.

A key reason why he was brought back to his native north-west by United was Omar Berrada’s appointment as chief executive. The pair worked together at City and there was a high degree of mutual respect, supported by the – now tainted – achievements of the club. Wilcox was given the title technical director and was supposed to work under the experienced sporting director Dan Ashworth, who held similar roles at Brighton and Newcastle but lasted only five months under Ratcliffe, earning Wilcox a rapid promotion.

Some United staff in place when Wilcox arrived grew frustrated at the number of former City Football Group appointments being made. United had got plenty wrong over the years but continued to thrive in certain aspects, so trying to turn the club into a copy of one of their fiercest rivals grated.

Wilcox was influential in the recruitment of Ruben Amorim, who had a specific way of playing but not the players to carry out his demands. The experiment failed , accelerated by a breakdown in relationship between the head coach and Wilcox, who did not see eye-to-eye on tactics, among other things.

When it comes to players there is increasingly a focus on Premier League experience with Wilcox; this summer Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba arrived from top-flight English clubs for a combined £155m. The midfield did require an overhaul, with Casemiro leaving and Manuel Ugarte, currently injured, never reaching the requisite level. That outlay, however, meant there was no money for a left-back or backup striker, leaving fans eager for an explanation. In the defeat at Atlético, Carrick played the 20-year-old centre-back Ayden Heaven out of position to cover Luke Shaw’s latest absence, summing up the shallowness of the squad.

Ratcliffe, the minority owner, is on record as saying he has a lot of time for Wilcox, “When I listen to Jason speak, I get what he’s saying,” he told the Times in March 2025. “He’s a warm character, he’s got a sense of humour, he knows what he’s talking about.” At matches, the pair can be often found sitting next to one another in discussion. Ratcliffe has displayed a ruthless business approach since investing in United, but removing Wilcox would be one of the more difficult personal decisions. Their relationship is strong and making a change would be bold. With finances likely to be tight in January, the planning at this stage is for next summer and who is best to navigate it.

If results continue to be substandard, Ratcliffe and Berrada will be forced to consider their options. Wilcox’s bond with the pair is important but Carrick has a lot more credit in the bank with a fanbase that wields power and has strong reservations over the director of football. Removing Wilcox would be the more widely popular decision but also an acceptance of failure from the top brass. Ratcliffe once said Wilcox had the “best eyes in the club” but he cannot be blinded by the truth.

title: Wilcox the target again in another damaging Man Utd fallout
text:
It is almost 10 months since Jason Wilcox was in the line of fire when Ruben Amorim gave the explosive post-match news conference at Leeds that triggered his dismissal.

Amorim was furious Manchester United's director of football had subtly advised him to change tactics for the previous game against Wolves.

"I will do my job and every department, the scouting department, the sporting director, needs to do theirs," said Amorim.

Less than 24 hours after that chiding, Amorim was sacked, and the focus was on the part Wilcox played in that.

This time Lisandro Martinez was doing the firing and had a target in mind.

He might have got the job title slightly wrong, but there was no doubting who Martinez meant after the 2-0 loss to Atletico Madrid when he said: "I expect more from our technical director."

There is no doubting either that Martinez knew what he was saying.

Working as a post-match interviewer for US broadcaster CBS, legendary former United goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel tried to steer Martinez away from discussion about his old club's summer transfer window on four occasions. Each time, the Argentina defender refused to be deflected.

"We don't have the best squad at the moment compared to other top teams," said Martinez.

"I'm not going to close my mouth. We need more ambition. If we don't say the truth, nothing will change."

During the summer, BBC Sport was told by dressing room sources the club needed to sign more players than the three - Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans, Carlos Baleba - who eventually arrived, and it was "fairly obvious" where they needed to be - left-back and striker.

Another source with extensive knowledge of the inner workings at Old Trafford describes the current situation as "a mess".

Man Utd defender Martinez issues scathing attack on board

Quiz: Do you remember the big names who took aim at football club chiefs?

Martinez said he felt it was important to speak out the way he did. Many United fans are delighted he went down that path, and the defender was highlighting inadequacies in the club's leadership structure.

However, there are a couple of other basic realities.

The first is that Martinez's contract expires at the end of the season. United have the option to extend it by another year.

By being so outspoken against senior figures at the club, was he trying to ensure that option is not triggered, which would allow him to leave for nothing in the summer, or, potentially, for a lower fee in January?

Martinez is good friends with Atletico Madrid defender Cristian Romero and the international colleagues spoke after last night's game. Romero was similarly forceful against the Tottenham hierarchy last season.

Also, while the vast majority of United fans may agree with Martinez, internally his comments create a problem.

Most obviously, Carrick, having deflected questions about the defender's outburst in the immediate aftermath of the game, will face more probing on the matter when he speaks to the media before Sunday's trip to Leeds.

Any players lined up to talk around the Elland Road trip will be similarly quizzed. When Tielemans was asked about it by Amazon Prime on Tuesday night, he replied with a "no comment". Given the comments about recruitment, he would clearly be within his rights to ask Martinez outright "did you mean me?"

Carrick has to manage the delicate dressing room dynamic at a point when he needs a collective focus on trying to win enough matches to keep him in a job.

Sources who know the United boss well are adamant there is no better person to handle the turmoil, and it is at times of crisis like this that his innate calmness is a major strength.

However, after five games without a win, it is a problem Carrick could do without.

Firstly, it must be pointed out Wilcox is going nowhere.

United sources say the 55-year-old is not in any danger of losing his job.

The club's recruitment department is working on potential targets for January given it is accepted the strategy of not signing left-back competition for Luke Shaw and striking support for Benjamin Sesko was flawed.

Both players have missed matches already this term, with Sesko sidelined for an indefinite period after suffering a recurrence of the shin issue that flared up in May and prevented him from playing any part in United's pre-season matches.

Unlike other major footballing countries on the continent, there is no expectation for sporting or technical directors to speak to the media.

Former United sporting director Dan Ashworth did it once during his five months at the club and was sitting alongside chief executive Omar Berrada.

Wilcox's only extensive interview since he was appointed in April 2024 has been with United's in-house media, when a couple of answers stood out.

"I am a coach at heart," said the former Blackburn Rovers and Leeds United winger, who spent several years working in coaching at Manchester City's academy.

"I am a coach inside, even though I know I have a different job now. That is a strength in my role, but it also causes me a bit of a problem because I always want to interfere in what the managers are doing."

Regarding his strategy for dealing with stress, Wilcox said: "My wife will know when I am bogged down with frustration. When I re-energise, I do it on my own. Me and the dog, walking."

Wilcox has only spoken briefly to the media after matches on a couple of occasions: after the 2-1 win at Crystal Palace last November, when he told journalists to "trust the process"; then again in Gothenburg after the pre-season encounter with Paris St-Germain when he enthused about the potential pairing of Tielemans and skipper Bruno Fernandes.

Recruitment was praised in summer 2025, when Senne Lammens was signed ahead of Emi Martinez, who was Amorim's preference, and Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo, plus Sesko, reinvigorated United's attack.…

title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
text:
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.

The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.

Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.

The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US.

Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increase over time.

For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.

Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).

It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.

The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.

There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.

If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.

Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.

Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.

Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.

Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices.

Car fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.

In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau or Labor Statistics.

Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.

Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher.

At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year.

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.

Shortly after the latest inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by the same amount - 3.6% - in 2027.

The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.

The cost of living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72m people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.

Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.

While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.

Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.

In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.

Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.

Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.

While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years.

During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.

Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.

Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.

It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.

A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.

Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.

Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

'We have been in touch with the rider directly and apologised' – ITA responds to Valentina Cavallar's post about doping control on day her mother died
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
The International Testing Agency (ITA) have apologised to Austrian rider Valentina Cavallar after an anti-doping officer arrived to test her following the death of her mother, while at the same time defending their procedures.

A doping control officer arrived at Cavallar's home "just a few hours" after her mother's death in September, she wrote, and the test was carried out with her mother in the next room.

"It was a moment that made me reflect on how easily we can forget that behind every athlete, there is a human being with a life, a family and emotions that do not simply disappear when the responsibilities of professional sport begin," added the SD Worx-Protime racer.

The ITA stated that Cavallar informed the doping control officer of her mother's death shortly after their arrival, but noted that she raised "no concerns or requests to postpone or discontinue the control" at the time.

"The International Testing Agency (ITA) extends its sincere condolences to Valentina Cavallar and her family following the loss of her mother," the statement to read.

"Since learning about the circumstances of the sample collection which took place on 5 September 2026 on Valentina Cavallar, the ITA looked into the context of the test.

"Neither the ITA nor the Doping Control Officer (DCO) were aware of the rider’s personal situation prior to arriving at her home. The DCO was informed of her mother’s passing upon arrival. According to the information gathered by the ITA since the rider’s Instagram post [Monday], Ms Cavallar and her family cooperated fully with the procedure, and no concerns or requests to postpone or discontinue the control were raised at the time or afterwards."

Under cycling's whereabouts system, riders must submit their location during a 60-minute period each day when they will be available for testing. Cavallar's situation occurred was a result of tragic coincidence, which the ITA acknowledged as an "exceptionally sensitive situation."

The doping control officer "endeavoured to pursue the procedure as discreetly, respectfully and swiftly as possible" with Cavallar and her family's support, the ITA's statement continued, before the organisation noted that it had reached out to her to apologise directly for the situation and any distress caused.

"We fully recognise that undergoing a doping control in these circumstances has added to her distress experienced at an extraordinarily painful time. We have been in touch with the rider directly and apologised.

"The ITA remains committed to ensuring that the protection of clean sport goes hand in hand with respect, compassion and care for athletes.

"We will also continue to always encourage athletes to report any concerns either during or after a doping control, so the ITA can take the appropriate measures to ensure a proportionate balance between the fight against doping and every athlete’s right to privacy and wellbeing."

title: Car enters course during Dutch race just four days after rider safety protest at Il Lombardia
author: James Moultrie
text:
A driver entered Wednesday's race route with around 70km to go just ahead of the breakaway, going in the same direction. Fortunately an in-race marshal was able to direct the green car to the side of the road from a motorbike, where it pulled over, allowing the three breakaway riders to pass safely.

Thankfully, the peloton were 1:44 behind, so by the time they reached the spot where the car was, it had already been diverted off the course. But it's the latest in a run of incidents which forced the riders' hands before the last Monument of the season.

Remco Evenepoel led the protest and delayed start in Italy on Saturday, giving a speech in which he said: "We want to make this statement because there's too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race. Unfortunately we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us, so we want to make this statement to show to the world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or literally dying in what we like the most to do."

Since his death, non-race vehicles have entered the route at the Giro dell'Emilia and Coppa Bernocchi , with a police motorbike going the wrong way during Tre Valli Varesine also knocking two of Tom Pidcock's Pinarello Q36.5 teammates out of the race.

Racing continued on Wednesday with Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep) taking the win on the impacted Eneco Tour stage, but it's the latest in a run of shocking incidents just this year which forced the riders to take a stand at Il Lombardia.

At the same time as Evenepoel spoke, a scheduled shared statement was released by many of the riders in the professional peloton, in which they called for action from cycling's governing body, the UCI, and race organisers.

"As riders, we stand united against the unnecessary risk our lives are being subjected to," it read.

"[Last] week alone, there were multiple incidents of vehicles on race courses. Two riders crashed when they hit a motorbike who was driving the wrong way on the race route. Luckily both escaped with cuts and bruises, it could have been so much worse.

"This summer, a life was tragically lost to exactly this kind of failure. We will not stand for this any longer. Riders race at high speed with little protection, and we depend on the UCI and race organisers to secure the roads. That responsibility is not being met.

"We are calling for the UCI and race organisers to take accountability and act. That means a serious, open conversation between riders, race organisers and the UCI resulting in concrete changes to how race routes are secured and managed.

"After five minutes, we raced as normal. We did not want to affect the race, only to show what riders can do when we stand as one. We love this sport. We respect the race organisers. We want to race hard and put on a show for our fans. However most importantly we want to come home safe to our loved ones."

title: Giro del Veneto: Alessandro Covi pulls off first win of 2026 with well-timed sprint
author: Alasdair Fotheringham
text:
An exceptionally long uphill drive for the line netted Jayco-AlUla racer Alessandro Covi a small bunch sprint victory on home soil in the Giro del Veneto on Wednesday.

Covi began his move some 300 metres to go on Vicenza's Monte Berico, and the Italian climber narrowly fended off a almost equally persistent Uno-X Mobility's Anthon Charmig to claim his first victory since a stage of the Vuelta a Asturias last year.

UAE Team Emirates-XRG had dominated proceedings in a tightly controlled bunch in the last 50 kilometres, first with Pavel Sivakov and then with World Champion Brandon McNulty. But their designated contender, France's Benoit Cosnefrôy, could not repeat teammate Isaac del Toro's win in Veneto last year and finally had to settle for third.

Covi's home triumph also ended a lengthy drought on victories for Jayco-AlUla, whose last win was a stage of 2026 Tour de France with Mauro Schmid.

Asked by race TV about his lengthy wait for a victory this year with Jayco-AlUla, Covi explained that it was impossible to predict when success would happen.

"You never know, it's difficult to win, but if it happens in October it's still a big victory," he said.

"Also, it's a nice race, I already did it a few times. It's the end of the season, a lot of the guys are tired - me too.

"But it's nice to win with a new jersey, [it's been] ten months before this victory arrived but it's a really nice victory."

In a race which took a long time to come alive, an early attack by eight low-profile riders, all of them from Continental or Club level bar one, Tommaso Nencini (Solution Tech Nippo Rali), was the standout feature of the first 100 kilometres.

Together with Nencini, the strongest in the all-Italian break - Francisco Carollo and his Swatt Club teammate, Giacomo Garavaglia , Kevin Pezzo Rosola and Thomas Rossetti (both General Store - Essegibi - F.Lli Curia), Leonardo Volpato (Campana Imballaggi - Morbiato - Trentino) and Riccardo Lorello (S.C. Padovani Polo Cherry Bank) had a two-minute lead on the pack as they passed the finish line for the first time in Vicenza, positioned two thirds of the way up the kilometre-long Monte Berico.

Having enjoyed their time in the warm autumn sunshine, with three local laps of five and 44 kilometres to go the last of the early breakaways was caught, in large part thanks to Pavel Sivakov's aggressive patrolling on the front of the bunch. Whilst a subsequent brief dig by Andrea Petrobon (Polti-VisitMalta) kept viewers entertained, there was little sense, though, that the main contenders were ready - or perhaps even able, given UAE's iron grip on proceedings - to make a long-distance move.

Once Petrobon was sucked in on the second-to-last ascent of the Monte Berico, the same grinding-down process continued, as UAE both controlled their most dangerous rivals with a high pace that simultaneously saw numerous riders shed out the back.

Pounding up the Arcugnano, the other, far gentler, main ascent on the circuit, Sivakov kept up the hard work whilst the white jersey of teammate and World Champion Brandon McNulty was never far away, either.

Tudor and Uno-X Mobility were the keenest to lead into the last full ascent of the Berico, but their efforts to break UAE's long stranglehold on affairs proved limited. Rather, Sivakov delivered one final effort, and as the bunch romped through the finish line and over the top of the grinding, steady climb, McNulty himself tried to go clear.

The American's flick-of-the-elbow gesture to co-attacker Christian Scaroni (XDS-Astana) to come through failed to spark enough of a reaction, though for his plan to work out, and instead there was a general regrouping. Marc Hirschi (Tudor) then rolled back the years with a searing uphill move, and while McNulty visibly sat up, both Hirschi and Fabio Christen (Pinarello-Q36.5) were able to go clear.

The two had a gap of almost ten seconds as they blasted along the undulating Arcugnano and McNulty then delivered yet another counter-attack to try and bridge across. However, the American could not make it alone, his rainbow jersey meaning he was heavily marked.

Even so, with six kilometres to go McNulty's constant accelerations did bring the bunch up to the two Swiss riders, and the American then almost single handedly ensured things remained together en route to the final, partial ascent of the Berico.

The front group of some 60 or 70 riders was still loosely together on the foot of the climb, as McNulty continued to drive away, only dropping back with 400 metres to go. However, Covi then launched a very long, sustained acceleration that saw the Italian both draw out the main group and stay ahead. Then whilst Charmig pushed Covi hard and Cosnefrôy and Christen were closing in fast, the 28-year-old Italian still had both the energy and resistance to manage to keep his rivals behind his front wheel all the way to the line.

"[Teammate Andrea] Vendrame was the guy we had for the sprint, but in the middle of the circuit, he came to me, said he didn't feel good and I should wait for the sprint," Covi explained afterwards about how he'd taken a much-needed victory for himself and the team.

"So I did exactly what he said, I never moved, I was always in the first group and I just tried for the sprint, and then I won. So that was super nice of Andrea, too."

title: Eneco Tour: Tim Merlier wins stage 1 sprint in Ede ahead of Dylan Groenewegen
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep) sailed to victory on stage 1 at Eneco Tour launching a long-range sprint on the final 400 metres which had no reply from rivals.

Dylan Groenewegen (Unibet Rose Rockets) trailed in second while Gerben Thijssen (Alpecin-Premier Tech) took third ahead of Visma-Lease a Bike's Christophe Laporte.

The win moved Merlier 27 positions in the GC standings, now fifth overall. The top four positions held firm with just a two-second gap established from the opening prologue, Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) in the leader's jersey. Wessel Mouris (Unibet Rose Rockets) remains in second place, Laporte in third and Merlier's teammate Ethan Hayter in fourth.

Once at the flamme rouge, Soudal-QuickStep went into formation for Merlier on the right side of the course. At the final 90-degree corner with 400 metres to go, Nils Eekhoff from Picnic PostNL took the lead with riders from Unibet Rose Rockets, Visma-Lease a Bike and Alpecin just behind. Merlier exploded past them all and won by several bike lengths.

"It was quite hectic [in the final kilometre], and then we speed up, a really high speed. It was also difficult to find each other, but in the end we did really well," Merlier said about scoring his 13th victory on Wednesday.

"They bring me to a good position, and then I choose what I'm gonna do in the last 500 metres. I think it was a bit of a risk to go a bit further, but in the end, I can go in the slipstream, and speed up from behind the other guys. This kind of finish suits me really well."

After the 3.1km prologue to set the leaderboard, stage 1 took place with a flat 40-kilometre circuit on the north side of Ede tackled three times for 120km.

The peloton began the opening kilometres sizing up each other under the sunny skies, with the seven WorldTour teams massing at the front. Then a trio from a Dutch Continental squads were allowed to accelerate away - Johan Dorussen (Metec-SOLARWATT p/b Mantel), Rick Ottema (EEW-VDK Cyclingteam) and Luke Verburg (Azerion-Villa Valkenburg). .

Once on the second circuit, the three riders took shares in maintaining their breakaway and built a gap of 3:00. On the approach to Ede for the final loop, the gap began to fade as the peloton sensed time to position their fast men.

The breakaway trio scooped up all the bonuses at the intermediate sprint with 24km to go, but the peloton was only 15 seconds back with 15km to go. A wall of sprint teams, led by Soudal-QuickStep, Picnic PostNL and Unibet Rose Rockets, spread across the road and charged from behind to end the breakaway with 11km to go.

As the shadows began to stretch across the road with the sun beginning to fade in late afternoon, the peloton seemed to settle down on the next four kilometres heading back into the city limits. Visma-Lease a Bike edged to the front to support Christophe Laporte alongside Soudal-QuickStep while Unibet Rose Rockets held position on an outside line for Wessel Mouris with Lotto-Intermarché sending riders up. Lidl-Trek was there for race leader Jakob Söderqvist, biding their time as the finish neared.

It wasn't until 2km to go that the wide procession began to fracture, Soudal-QuickStep amping up the action. This straight run led to a defining sharp left-hand corner onto Arnhemseweg for the final 400 metres.

On that final corner, Merlier used the slipstream of his teammate Bert Van Lerberghe to vault from sixth position to first as he flew down the straightaway for the victory.

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Stay diligent’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
Four of the five Knicks starters didn’t board a plane north of the border, the fifth one didn’t play basketball on Tuesday, and it all showed badly.

New York will host a preseason game for one final time on Thursday before dressing in gold for Tuesday’s banner night.

Here’s the latest from Mike, James, and Miles.

On the Knicks’ performance and defensive shortcomings in their 50-point preseason loss to Toronto:

“It’s not necessarily what’s on the scoreboard at that particular time. It is: are you doing the right things to be better and/or get better? And in the first half, what I was most disappointed in was we weren’t putting bodies on bodies. Fifteen second-chance points in one half is not good. Thirty fast-break points in one half is not good.

“And then the way they sped us up, and us not necessarily touching the paint and trying to spray it and/or making quick decisions is not good. So that’s what I was most disappointed in in the first half. I really didn’t care about the score, especially with the group we had on the floor.”

On how James Wiseman has developed since his time with the Warriors:

“Back then, obviously, he was talented but he was really raw in terms of his ability and feel on the court. It’s obviously a lot higher now, but he’s also been humbled a little bit with the challenges and the adversity he’s gone through in his career. He understands how hard it is. That obviously is different now than what it was back then.”

On Wiseman’s growth and understanding of how quickly NBA opportunities can disappear:

“Everything was new to him. He was a wide-eyed young puppy and now he’s a little bit more seasoned with the knowledge of, ‘This is not gonna be easy and opportunities can come and go like that.’”

On appreciating his opportunity to compete for a roster spot with the Knicks:

“It’s a blessing to just be here. Really just being able to go out there, enjoy myself, have fun, just keep working. Stay diligent.”

On overcoming injuries and adversity throughout his NBA career:

“It’s been a lot. Really just putting God first. Staying down, grinding every single day and just taking one day at a time. That’s really all you can do, just really control what you can.”

On what he has learned about himself through his career struggles:

“Really just being able to stay resilient through the process and really just staying persistent as well.”

On how his athleticism can help him earn the Knicks’ final roster spot:

“Just being able to use my athleticism. Being able to put my head on the rim every single time, run the floor and really just being vocal.”

On the Knicks’ 50-point preseason loss to the Raptors:

“You never want to lose in that way. But at the same time, we just gotta move on. Preseason is for those reasons. Missing eight of our guys, you just want to come out there and have a positive mindset. Go out there and play hard. There were things we could’ve definitely done better, but they’re a playoff team and you add a Hall of Famer with them.”

title: Track World Championships: Lorena Wiebes triumphs again in scratch race, Taylor Phinney returns with USA team pursuit squad
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
As was the case last year, rainbow jerseys were awarded for the women's scratch race and both the men's and women's team sprints, while qualification rounds for the men's and women's team pursuits came earlier in the day.

Lorena Wiebes scored the first gold of the Championships in the women's scratch race, while the Netherlands won the men's team sprint for the third year in succession and the home nation triumphed in the women's team sprint.

Read on for full reports and results from all of Wednesday's action.

Dutch star Lorena Wiebes took home the first rainbow jersey of the week, but only just, as she prevailed for the third year in a row at the scratch race. At the line, Wiebes edged out Lara Gillespie by centimetres to hang on and win as the Irishwoman launched from behind to take silver.

The 40-lap race saw a host of riders sweep to the front and up the pace as Wiebes' rivals sought to throw her off her stride ahead of the final. She lay in wait further back, comfortable in her position as she waited for the closing sprint.

After 10 minutes of racing, the riders reached the final 10 laps, with no big move at the front. With seven laps to go, France's Valentine Fortin leapt first as Wiebes jumped from the group to chase.

A regrouping followed as Wiebes dropped back again, and Belgium's Hélène Hesters led it into the final four laps. Wiebes came back, though, coming around the outside to hit the front again with two laps to go.

Gillespie was on her wheel, taking Portugal's Maria Martins with her as the lead trio opened up a gap on the rest on the final lap. Wiebes led around the final bend, but faded in the final metres before the line. Gillespie closed in but just missed out on passing the Dutchwoman, while Martins finished just behind the pair to take bronze.

"I think it's quite crazy. Of course you always go for the win, but it's always harder and harder to repeat it. Today was also really close. Lara came really close, but it was enough to win, and that's all I need," Wiebes said after her triumph.

"I think at the end, I needed to start my sprint a bit too early, but you also need to adapt to that situation, and I tried as good as possible. Lara was also really fast today, but I'm happy it was enough. That's the thing with scratch racing; it's also about positioning and tactics, not only the speed in the legs."

The Netherlands (Jeffrey Hoogland, Harrie Lavreysen, Roy van den Berg), reigning world champions and unbeaten in this event since 2023, re-established themselves as favourites in the qualifying and first rounds, going quickest at both to sweep into the final round.

Australia (Daniel Barber, Ryan Elliott, Leigh Hoffman) ran them close, though, heading into the gold medal race with a mere 0.115-second deficit after improving on their qualifying run.

China (Zhiheng Jin, Zhiwei Li, Qi Liu) and Japan (Yoshitaku Nagasako, Minato Nakaishi, Kaiya Ota), second and third in the qualifying round, completed the top four in the first round, both coming through with a near-0.2-second gap to fifth-placed Trinidad and Tobago.

In the final, China and Japan battled for bronze, and the home nation had the upper hand early on. They passed the 250-metre mark 0.035 seconds up on Japan, who looked less organised from the start, with a rider dropping behind. China duly capitalised on that error to race to a 0.947-second advantage after 625 metres, and they finished it off to win bronze, 1.255 seconds ahead of Japan.

In the gold medal race, it was reigning world champions, the Netherlands, versus last year's bronze medallists, Australia. The Dutch slipped behind early on, though, losing 0.219 seconds in the opening 250 metres, but they closed it to almost a dead heat over the next 250, starting the final run just 0.005 seconds off their rivals. A tense closing 250 metres saw the Dutch turn it around to win the rainbow jersey once again, finishing the race 0.516 seconds quicker than silver medallists Australia.

"It's an amazing feeling. I've got seven world titles, and they've got eight. It means a lot. We've been training very hard the last year, and when everything comes together at the most important race, it's amazing," said Van den Berg, before Hoogland described the final push in the race.

"I was just mad going into the final, so I gave it my all in the last lap. I threw everything I knew out of the window and just started pushing the pedals," he said.

Lavreysen said he was happy to win again after a long drought for the team, saying, "I'm very happy we can start the [Olympic] qualification with a win. We didn't win any races since last World Championships, so I'm really happy we can keep the jersey and show it this year."

The two nations made it through the first round, with China on top by 0.280 seconds as Germany (Lea Friedrich, Pauline Grabosch, Clara Schneider) and the Individual Neutral Athletes (Iana Burlakova, Ekaterina Evlanova, Alina Lysenko) finished with the third- and fourth-best times to make the battle for bronze.

One major surprise in the first round came as the reigning champions, the Netherlands (Kimberley Kalee, Hetty van de Wouw, Steffie van der Peet), missed out on the final, finishing fifth, 0.048 seconds off fourth place.

In the bronze medal race, Germany started slow, losing 0.310 seconds to the Individual Neutral Athletes in the first 250 metres. title: Driving test waits fall to two-year low - but still average 20 weeks
text:
Waiting times for driving tests have dropped below 20 weeks for the first time since November 2024, according to official figures.

But learner drivers in September still had to wait an average of 19.7 weeks, or around five months, for a practical test.

The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) has been trying to cut waiting times and clear a backlog which began during the Covid pandemic in 2020.

Commenting on the agency's progress, one driving instructor told the BBC: "I don't think this is anything to boast about."

The DVSA initially had hoped to reduce the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible - with waits not expected to fall to seven weeks until next autumn .

The DVSA conducted 191,682 practical driving tests in September, with more than half of those passing.

Learner drivers have repeatedly told the BBC how a lack of access to driving tests has limited their freedom, education and job prospects.

Until earlier this year, many learner drivers chose to pay inflated prices to access driving tests being resold by third party providers who'd used automated programmes, or bots, to block book tests before learners could access them.

But a number of changes were made to the test booking system earlier this year by the DVSA to stop the system being exploited. Now, only the learner driver is able to book their driving test.

Sophie Stuchfield, a driving instructor in Watford, told the BBC: "Whilst the re-selling of tests does seem to have stopped, which is a massive positive, they've still failed to recruit enough examiners to cope with demand."

She didn't believe that the slight fall in numbers for waiting times "is anything to boast about", adding that in many areas the wait for a driving test when booking is 21 weeks.

"On many occasions, my drivers wake up at 5.45am on a Monday, only to not end up with a test as when they click on something, by the time they put their details in, they are told the test has already been taken."

Sophie added that the waiting time to get a test meant that many learner drivers "who haven't even started driving lessons will book a test knowing it's 5 months away", putting themselves and the instructor under a lot of pressure.

Justin Madders, the minister for roads, said the government "inherited record waiting times and a significant backlog".

"While driving test waiting times are still not where we want them to be, these figures show real progress is being made," he added.

A DVSA spokesperson said the agency was "committed to reducing waiting times" and that "examiner numbers are at their highest level since November 2017".

"But we know there's more to do and we won't stop until every learner can get a test slot when they need one, wherever they're learning to drive," the spokesperson added.

title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
author: Melody Schreiber
text:
Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr

Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.

The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr , secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.

Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.

But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing , where he referred to the study as “tests”.

“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.

“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.

He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).

The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year.

The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints.

“When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”.

She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.”

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.”

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.

In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.

“It’s completely unethical that this trial is even proposed,” because a safe and effective vaccine has been available for decades, said BK Titanji, a researcher at Emory University.

It’s “reassuring” to see Guinea-Bissau pushing back on the trial, Titanji said, adding: “A study like this one needs the highest level of ethical scrutiny. You are going to be conducting a study on the most vulnerable population, which is newborn babies, in a country that is resource constrained.”

When Titanji recently applied for approval of a collaborative study in Cameroon, she had to include extensive documentation in her application – and it’s a survey, not medical research on human subjects, she said. “I can’t come to Emory’s IRB [institutional review board] and just be like: ‘I got permission from Cameroon.’ I have to provide the document.”

The researchers should release these documents and an updated protocol showing how the study would be conducted, she said.

Experts have decried the African experiment as “ horribly unethical and cruel ”, “ neo-colonialist ” and “ damaging ”.

“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”

It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.

Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”

It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The ​study has ⁠not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.

At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.…

title: Acosta proposes new idea for monitoring tyre pressure in MotoGP
Wayfair among firms fined millions for misleading sales tactics
text:
Wayfair is among three firms which have been fined £6m in total by the competition watchdog for illegally using misleading sales tactics – with some customers set to receive refunds.

The online furniture retailer was fined £4.8m for misleading customers with time-limited offers, while online electronics seller Appliances Direct was fined £1.2m for the same practice, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) said.

Meanwhile, Gold's Gym has been fined £48,000 for not telling customers the total price of its memberships.

It and Appliances Direct have been ordered to refund customers a total of £440,000. Wayfair and Appliances Direct said the CMA's fines were disproportionate.

Gold's Gym has been contacted for comment.

Thousands of Appliances Direct customers will receive refunds of £25 each on average while 726 Gold's Gym customers will get refunds of up to £50, according to the CMA.

The watchdog said customers do not need to take any action and both companies will contact those affected customers about refunds.

Appliances Direct has been told to pay refunds by 11 March, while Gold's Gym has been given a deadline of 29 March.

The CMA said Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym had "engaged constructively" with its investigation. They all admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early, it added.

The watchdog said their co-operation reduced the firms' fines by 40%.

The CMA's fines are the result of an investigation it launched last November into online pricing .

Eight firms under investigation over online pricing

AA and BSM ordered to refund learner drivers for hidden fees

A Wayfair spokeswoman said the penalty was "excessive" but that "we take the CMA's findings seriously and we chose to settle so we can continue to focus on serving our customers".

Nick Glynne, chief executive of Buy it Direct, which owns Appliances Direct and several other online retailers, accepted that its practices were wrong, but said the firm should have simply been given "a rap on the knuckles" instead.

Glynne said the CMA's process for calculating the fine was a "black box" and that it only settled because appealing was too expensive, accusing the watchdog of pressure tactics.

"When one body is investigator, prosecutor, judge and jury, it needs an exceptional commitment to fairness, restraint and proportionality. That is not what we experienced," he added.

Hayley Fletcher, senior director for consumer protection at the CMA, said: "At a time when many households are carefully managing their budgets, people shouldn't lose out because of misleading sales tactics.

"Businesses must treat their customers fairly and make sure they comply with the law - or risk hefty fines."

The CMA's investigation found that the three companies had misled customers in different ways.

Wayfair had advertised products as if they would disappear the next day, through phrases like "Here Today, Gone Tomorrow" and countdown timers.

However, the CMA said many products remained available at the same price or lower after the stated deadline, meaning the time-limited offer was false.

Meanwhile, the regulator said Appliances Direct had automatically opted customers into services such as recycling old machines.

Gold's Gym was fined for failing to include joining fees in the total price of gym memberships or not making its total price clear to customers, the CMA said.

title: Former Zwift Academy winner Emily Dixon moves up to Canyon-SRAM WorldTour team
author: Alasdair Fotheringham
text:
Promising young Australian rider Emily Dixon has been confirmed as part of the Canyon-SRAM WorldTour team for the next two seasons.

A former Zwift Academy winner back in 2024 , Dixon has been racing for the last two years with the Canyon-SRAM Generation squad. She will now make a further key move in her career, into Canyon's top racing team.

Twelfth in the 2026 under-23 women's World Championships road race and the winner of two stages in the Gracia Orlová race back in April, also leading it for several days, Dixon has shown considerable promise this season. Her consistency in longer events was on display, too, when she took third in the toughest stage of the Tour Féminin International des Pyrénées, finally ending sixth overall and second in the BYR rankings.

Dixon will now make the senior Canyon-SRAM WorldTour team her squad for 2027. That's just two years after she beat more than 100,000 other contenders for a Continental contract with Canyon-SRAM Generation, confirmed in March 2025, and before she has reached 20.

"They say ‘never stop dreaming’, and one dream was to be in Europe racing for a pretty cool team like Canyon-SRAM," Dixon said in a press release.

"Now, it’s another dream coming true to race for the WorldTeam. I didn’t think this would be possible before turning 20, so I think my younger self would be very proud.

"I knew when signing with Generation that WorldTour was what I wanted, but I wasn’t so satisfied with my 2025 season and didn’t quite expect to make the jump I have this year.

"So, in a way, I’ve surprised myself, and that’s why I’m a bit like, ‘Whoa, I’m signing WorldTour.’ I’m really happy with my progression."

"The team recognises that she’s a young rider, and I believe it’s good that she will be moving to WorldTour level in the same organisation," added Generation Team Manager and Sports Director Gosia Jasinska in the same press release.

"I’ve already talked with the WorldTeam sport directors, and they’ve also worked with her already, so they know it’s not necessary to put pressure on her shoulders because she’s the kind of person who is already hard on herself.

"In her first year at least, it will be a big step to ride in the WorldTour, but I think racing amongst the top names and for strong leaders will be a pleasure and very fun for her. Still, I think she could definitely find some opportunities for herself."

Discussing her move to senior level in Canyon-SRAM and how it came about, Dixon added that "I think what’s changed has been my mindset."

"And that seems really cliché, but I think for th e road race at [the Australian] Nationals" - taking sixth on the day behind Mackenzie Coupland - "I really focused on my mentality as I realised how much my mind would affect my racing. That road race proved it to me and kind of unlocked the power of my mind, which has really helped me this year, especially with positioning.

As for 2027 and her first season at WorldTour level, she said: "I want to be a really good teammate – that sounds a little bit stupid, but I really want to be there for the team.

"I want to go to the races and do exactly what I’ve been asked to do. I also want to be in a team that succeeds, and Canyon-SRAM does that very well, so I’d love to be part of that atmosphere while learning from everyone much more experienced than me.

"I’m very keen to put on the WorldTeam jersey and for it to actually be mine – that’s so cool! It will say WorldTour, and that’s been my dream, and it’s actually going to be real."

title: Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears
text:
A civil servant is accused of earning almost £350,000 by juggling five full-time public sector roles - using sick notes and working from home to cope with the workload.

Kashim Chowdhury allegedly held multiple government jobs between February 2020 and September 2023, earning £350,000 overall.

The jury at Southwark Crown Court has been told he wore white make-up during a video call with his boss to try to look ill, but the make-up began peeling off his skin.

Chowdury, a 55-year-old from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud, which he denies. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

The jury was told that Chowdhury got jobs by making ''false representations'' about his employment status whilst applying. Over three years he held overlapping jobs at Tower Hamlets Council in east London, the Home Office, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency and the Department of Health and Social Care.

The jury was told that in 2023 his manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him to discuss his sick leave.

Ms Adams claims Chowdhury was wearing make-up on his face to appear ill - and that during the meeting the make-up started to separate on his forehead showing his real skin underneath. At the time of the call he is alleged to have been paid for five full time jobs.

Lucy Organ, for the prosecution, told the court: "There could be no doubt about it, the defendant had applied make-up to his face for this Teams meeting to try and pretend to his line manager that he was unwell.

"This almost laughable incident demonstrates, we say, quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit."

Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work from home culture that began during the Covid pandemic. The court was told that Chowdhury had told his employers that he had to work from home to care for his "unwell" mother.

But the prosecutor, Ms Organ, said his workload eventually became "too much to cope with" and his performance suffered.

The court heard that he was signed off work from some jobs due to "mixed anxiety and a depressive disorder", but he did not hand his sick note to all his employers.

Jurors heard that the alleged fraud came to light after the National Fraud Initiative alerted Defra to them.

title: Tour de France Boss Rejects Radical Idea to Cut Race to Two Weeks
author: ahood
text:
Christian Prudhomme, far left, pushed back against the idea of shortening the Tour de France. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Shrinking the Tour de France and the other grand tours to make room for the UCI ‘s controversial cycling overhaul?

No way, says Tour boss Christian Prudhomme.

“The Tour de France lasts three weeks, four weekends, and that’s perfectly fine,” Prudhomme told RMC Sport .

Prudhomme said he’s not interested in trimming cycling’s biggest race as proposals to shorten grand tours have kick-started a larger debate over the sport’s crowded calendar.

Speaking just days ahead of the unveiling of the 2027 Tour route, the Tour director defended its current format.

“That question concerns certain grand tours,” he said.

If the Tour vetoes any attempt to tweak the three-week format that dates back to its founding, that leaves the Giro d’Italia and Vuelta a España squarely on the chopping block.

But the bosses of cycling’s other grand tours aren’t buying into the idea to lose a weekend, either.

The debate comes as the UCI maps out potential reforms to professional cycling that could be rolled out by as soon as 2029.

Its “ Agenda 2030 ” consultation drew 55 submissions from teams, riders, organizers, federations, sponsors, manufacturers, and broadcasters.

Unveiled during the Montréal road worlds, the outline covers a broad range of issues that are on the table, including the calendar, cycling’s economic model, fan engagement, rider safety , and the integrity of results via doping controls .

Other ideas include a budget cap, sharing some commercial revenues, and improving broadcasting and marketing to reach today’s social-media savvy audience.

The UCI has since appointed Deloitte as a strategic adviser and the initial reform proposals are due to be presented in December, with the first measures potentially arriving in 2029.

One ideal outcome for backers of shorter grand tours is that the biggest stars like Tadej Pogačar, Jonas Vingegaard, and Remco Evenepoel might race all three rather than just obsessing on the Tour.

Right now, everything is on the table, and no firm proposals have been made.

But one of the most contentious ideas is to squeeze the grand tours into three weekends instead of four.

Some are floating the idea of shortening the Giro and Vuelta to 16 or 17 days, but keeping the Tour at 21 stages.

That idea is not without its supporters.

Some see the Giro and Vuelta dragging on too long sometimes, and the argument is that those extra days could free up some space on the calendar and help some races like Paris-Nice and Tirreno-Adriatico from overlapping.

The other grand tour bosses are having none of it.

New Giro director Luca Guercilena pushed back during an interview with Domestique at Il Lombardia.

“Grand tours must remain grand tours and the Giro d’Italia isn’t going to change. All three grand tours must be the same length,” the Italian said. “There can be no differences.”

The three-week grand tour format is one that grew organically over time. The first Tour in 1903 stretched across 19 days with just six monster stages averaging more than 400km, separated by rest days.

The Giro and later the Vuelta followed, and the grand tours settled into the now-familiar 21-stage, three-week rhythm.

For Guercilena, the brutal third week is the essential ingredient to what decides a grand tour winner.

“Cycling is an endurance sport, and it’s over three weeks that you can truly see if athletes are endurance riders,” he told RMC Sport . “We have no intention of changing that. I understand the UCI and its president, David Lappartient, who believe that overlapping races aren’t good for anyone. But the grand tours must remain three weeks long.”

Vuelta director Javier Guillén drew an equally firm line in a recent interview with MARCA .

“We are not in favor of eliminating any days, not even one. It’s true that the debate is ongoing, but at this time, it is not being discussed at any official or institutional level,” Guillén said.

The Giro and Vuelta have long defended their place alongside the Tour, and resisted any efforts to reduce the number of race days.

Of course, race organizers have a vested interest because every race day comes with lucrative host city start and finish fees, TV rights revenue, and fees from the publicity caravan.

“We believe that the days honoring the great icons of cycling should remain untouched, because otherwise we would all be worse off,” Guillén told the Spanish daily. “There’s no point in doing that.”

The Vuelta moved from April to September and now August in 1995, and the new place on the calendar has helped the Spanish grand tour grow in stature.

For 2027, however, the Vuelta will be contested after the UCI Road World Championships for the first time since the switch to make room for the second edition of “super worlds.”

title: Veneto Women: Liane Lippert rounds out 2026 season with solo summit victory in Italy
author: Alasdair Fotheringham
text:
The final one-day race of the 2026 elite women's season, Veneto Women, has been captured by German allrounder Liane Lippert (Movistar) in a late solo charge for the line.

Lippert roared home atop the short but punishing final ascent of Monte Berico in the northern Italian city of Vicenza, four seconds clear of closest pursuer Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek) . Local favourite Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L'IMAD) finished six seconds back.

After a flurry of early attacks, the race situation calmed down considerably, with Uno-X Mobility doing most of the work. More than half the total 106-kilometre distance had passed before a move of half a dozen riders managed to claw its way clear, the dangerous attack including the 2026 Trofeo Alfredo Binda and Giro dell'Emilia winners, Karlijn Swinkels (UAE Team L'IMAD) and Alessia Vigilia (Uno-X Mobility).

However, Movistar and Lidl-Trek ensured they never got more than 35 seconds advantage, and with 20 kilometres to go, the peloton was still compact, albeit fast shedding riders from the back on the relentlessly hilly finale.

Finally, another dangerous move emerged shortly after the second and final descent of the Arcugnano climb, this time containing Italian National Champion Longo Borghini and no less than three of her teammates in a group of eight - Mavi García, Eleonora Gasparrini and Swinkels. At the same time, Movistar were also well represented with Marlen Reusser, second last year ahead of Gasparrini, and her teammate Lippert. Also present were Noemi Ruegg (EF Education-Oatly) and Adegeest. With a 30-second advantage in the final five kilometres, it was clear one of the eight would claim the victory in the penultimate race of the 2026 women's calendar. Ultimately, Lippert was able to claim her first triumph of the season since the

Vuelta CV Féminas one-day race, all the way back in February, again with a late solo move.
